mcqs.question: Which of these is one of the concrete obligations that at-least-once delivery forces onto a consumer?
options: The consumer never needs to acknowledge messages at all
The consumer can safely assume messages always arrive in the order they were sent
The consumer's handlers must be idempotent, since redelivery is an expected, normal occurrence rather than a rare edge case
The consumer must reject any message it has seen before, discarding it silently
mcqs.explanation: Idempotent handlers are a direct requirement of at-least-once semantics, since redelivery isn't exceptional — it's expected. Acknowledgment is still required in most systems, ordering isn't guaranteed by at-least-once alone, and "discard silently" isn't the model — a redelivered message should be recognized and short-circuited to its prior result, not just dropped.

mcqs.question: Are at-least-once delivery and out-of-order delivery the same problem?
options: No, they're separate guarantees that often get lost together for the same underlying reason (retries and multiple partitions/consumers), and some systems provide one without the other
Yes, they are exactly the same guarantee described with different names
No, out-of-order delivery only happens with exactly-once systems, never at-least-once
Yes, because ordering is only relevant for messages larger than a certain size
mcqs.explanation: They're distinct guarantees, even though the same causes (retries, multiple consumers or partitions) often affect both — some systems give at-least-once with per-key ordering, others give neither, so a handler may need to be idempotent and order-independent depending on the system. They aren't identical, ordering issues aren't exclusive to exactly-once systems, and message size is irrelevant here.

mcqs.question: How should you decide how long to retain "already processed" dedup IDs before it's safe to forget them?
options: Retain them forever with no limit, since storage cost never matters for correctness
Delete them immediately after each message is processed, since the message won't be seen again
Retain them long enough to outlast the broker's or producer's actual maximum redelivery window, based on that system's specific retry configuration
Retain them for exactly 60 seconds in every system, regardless of configuration
mcqs.explanation: The correct retention window is tied to the specific messaging system's actual maximum redelivery delay — a deliberate decision, not a universal constant. Forgetting immediately reopens the duplicate-processing bug, and keeping everything forever has a real, avoidable storage cost; a fixed 60 seconds ignores that different systems have different redelivery windows.

mcqs.question: Why is it a mistake to assume a message broker's own offset or ack tracking alone prevents duplicate processing?
options: Offset tracking reflects what the broker has sent, not what the consumer has actually finished processing — a crash after processing but before committing the offset causes redelivery of already-completed work
Message brokers do not support offset tracking of any kind
Offset tracking only works for messages smaller than 1 KB
Offset tracking is deprecated in all modern messaging systems
mcqs.explanation: The gap is between "sent/acknowledged at the broker level" and "actually finished processing at the application level" — a crash in that gap causes redelivery of work that already completed, which broker-side tracking alone can't see. Offset tracking is a standard, widely supported feature, unrelated to message size, and not deprecated.
